utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Madam Registrar. Can we have the appearances for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, Counsel. For the Prosecution, Tecla Benjamin, Ekkehard Withopf, and Ruth Karper, the case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Withopf. Can we have the appearances for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours. On behalf of General Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, lead counsel; Stephane Bourgon, co-counsel; and Mirna Milanovic, legal assistant. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Kubura, Rodney Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and Mr. Mulalic, legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. After the weekend, the Chamber bids good afternoon to all those present, representatives of the Prosecution, the representatives of the accused, the accused, and the staff of this courtroom, and most particularly Madam Registrar, who's going to assist us this week. I also wish to greet the interpreters and the court reporter, as well as the security officers. Today we shall be continuing the hearing of a witness who testified on Friday, and his testimony will be continued by his cross-examination. I have learnt from the legal officer that the Defence has a statement to make, and I therefore give him the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Madam Judge. Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, Mr. President. Good afternoon. Before beginning the cross-examination of the witness who is before the Chamber, Lieutenant Colonel Chambers, we would like to have certain clarifications regarding the ruling of the Chamber regarding the duration of the cross-examination. Mr. President, our understanding of the decision of the Chamber was that the Defence should not take more than one and a half times the time used by the Prosecution for the cross-examination. This time is to be shared by representatives of both the Defence teams. Mr. President, this is a problem for us and for the following reasons: The witnesses that are before the Chamber that have appeared during the last two weeks and during next week are international witnesses, and these witnesses -- for these witnesses we will need more time than the Prosecution. The Prosecution had the advantage of having met the witness. They are their witnesses. And this particular witness has already told the Prosecution what he has to say in this Chamber, so there's -- so that is quite clear. The Defence has a number of documents to deal with, many of which have to do with international witnesses, and when an international witness appears, if the Prosecution uses only a single document prepared by that particular witness, it is a document that is -- that will be used in support of their case, as is normal, it is understandable that we on the Defence need to produce several documents which will require more time. You have certainly understood, Mr. President, that the questions discussed in this Chamber during the past few weeks and the week to come are at the very heart of the case, and therefore it is very important for us, for the Defence, to have adequate time to be able to properly use the witness of the opposing side to support their case and their submissions. Mr. President, I would like to indicate some statistics regarding the time used by the Defence up to now. We have made these calculations with the assistance of the registrar as well as our own records. According to those statistics, Mr. President, the total time used by the Prosecution up to now would be about 84 hours and 55 minutes; the total used by the Defence would be 57 hours and 6 minutes; therefore, we account for about 67 per cent of the time used by the Prosecution, and witness Garrod has not been included because he still hasn't been cross-examined, and also witness Chambers has not been included. As regard the number of witnesses that have been cross-examined by the Defence, we took less time than the Prosecution in 57 per cent of the cases, among whom three were international witnesses, and in 78 per cent of the cases we were shorter than the Prosecution, counting all the witnesses. And on 16 occasions, or in 22 per cent of the witnesses, we took more time than the Prosecution. Therefore, one out of two witnesses, or in 48 per cent of the cases, the Defence took less than half of the time used by the Prosecution. Finally, Mr. President, in order to be able to properly represent the interests of the accused and our case, without wishing to waste any time, we fully understand that if the Chamber believes that our arguments were not relevant or were presented in a way that causes a waste of time, then of course we can be interrupted and that would be quite normal. But we respectfully request to be allowed to have sufficient time to properly carry out our cross-examination. And we would like the decision of the Chamber to apply to the duration of the case as a whole, the Prosecution case. That is, once all the witnesses have been heard, we certainly will not have exceeded one and a half times the time used by the Prosecution. Otherwise, this could be prejudicial for us. As for today's witness, when the Chamber told us that we would be limited to 1 hour, 43 minutes for the cross-examination, we believe, Mr. President, that we need 2 hours, 30 minutes. That is for both accused. And as I explained a little earlier, the principal reason for the duration of the cross-examination is linked to the presentation and discussion of documents, which will be more numerous than those presented by the Prosecution during the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Bourgon. Does the other Defence team wish to say anything on this point? Mr. Dixon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Your Honours, as a practical matter, I understand, and the Prosecution will in all likelihood inform Your Honours of this, the second witness for today is no longer going to testify, and hence we may have enough time in any event to complete the cross-examination of Mr. Chambers and not have it affect the schedule. Other than that, Your Honours, we can say that on behalf of Mr. Kubura that we have considered our questions and will be able to complete our questions in the time allotted. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Dixon. Mr. Withopf, regarding this problem of substance, what are the observations of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, the Prosecution is a bit concerned that it becomes a pattern that Defence wishes to cross-examine the future Prosecution witnesses to an extent that is an obvious contradiction to the recent ruling of the Trial Chamber. The Prosecution is also a bit concerned that in the event this pattern continues, it may have a negative -- a very negative impact on the Prosecution's witness schedule, which has been communicated to both the Defence and the Chamber recently. For clarification, I wish to add one particular issue: It's not only the Prosecution in respect to the international witnesses which meets such witnesses in many instances; the Defence counsel also meet the Prosecution international witnesses prior to their testimony. Having said this, Mr. President, Your Honours, however, the Prosecution does not object - does not object - a Defence application to exceed the time limit, provided that certain conditions are met. Number one: The Defence should provide the Prosecution and Trial Chamber in detail reasons for extension of time to cross-examine Prosecution witnesses, reasons for which on their face appear to be reasonable; the Defence is allowed to only ask questions which appear to be relevant; and number three - and the Prosecution wishes to emphasise this last point - that the Prosecution at a later point during these proceedings - namely, once the Defence presents their witnesses - that the Prosecution is also at a case-by-case basis given more time to cross-examine the Defence witnesses. In respect to the today's cross-examination of the witness Chambers, Mr. President, Your Honours, the Prosecution does not object to the Defence application. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you, Mr. Withopf. The Chamber will withdraw for a couple of minutes to deliberate. Nevertheless, I wish to recall that we decided by a previous oral decision to limit the duration of the cross-examination to 50 per cent more than the time allotted to the Prosecution, which means that if the Prosecution takes one hour, the Defence will have an hour and a half; if the Prosecution takes two hours, the Defence will have three hours; that is, 50 per cent in addition to the time used by the Prosecution. That means the time should be multiplied by 1.5. The Defence attorneys, who have studied the time used up to now, tell us that in general terms the Defence has used less time than the Prosecution and that on 16 occasions, which is in 22 per cent of the cases, the Defence exceeded the time taken by the Prosecution. Concerning more specifically the international observers, the Defence tells us that in view of the fact that these witnesses are important, and as noted by the Defence we are at the core of the issue, the Defence would need to produce certain documents during the cross-examination, and this could take a little more time than the duration of the examination-in-chief. By way of a compromise, the Defence commits itself that should the time be exceeded for certain witnesses, the Defence promises that globally it will not take more than 50 per cent in addition to the time of the Prosecution regarding the totality of the witnesses. And in this particular case, we have 1 hour, 43 minutes for the Prosecution, the Defence tells us that they would need two and a half hours for the cross-examination. The Prosecution in reply tell us that they're aware of the problem, but that the Defence should not be used in a way that could prejudice the proper conduct of the proceedings. That is why we will withdraw for a few minutes and we will come back and render our ruling. --- Break taken at 2.34 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber has deliberated this matter, having heard the observations of the Defence, as well as of the Prosecution. At this stage it is the opinion of the Chamber that there's no need to reverse its previous decision, which means that the Defence is allowed to have 50 per cent more time than the Prosecution. On the other hand, due to exceptional circumstances linked to certain witnesses known as international witnesses, the Defence by a special submission may be authorised to exceed the time allotted it. During the cross-examination the questions put to the witness have to be relevant questions and must go to the heart of the matter, rather than being questions that have no effectiveness, because in that case everyone is wasting time and then one exceeds by far the time allotted. That is the first observation. The second is that as you have noted, in view of the highly technical and military nature of the questions put, the Chamber itself sometimes is prompted to ask questions, increasingly so, and following the questions put by the Chamber the Defence also has time to come back to certain matters. That time for the present is not being calculated, but this is time that is at your disposal. And, therefore, we believe when Judges ask questions at the end of the testimony, the Judges will again give you the floor to ask questions. The jurisprudence in this area indicates in general terms that after the Judges, in theory the parties should not ask any questions, except in two precise cases: If there are material errors made in the replies of the witness to the questions of the Judges; or because the witness is contributing new elements which have not been covered by the Defence and could be prejudicial to the accused. And that is the very specific jurisprudence in the area. However, up to the present the Chamber has quite liberally interpreted these Rules, allowing you to ask questions. So if the Judges take ten minutes for their questions - take ten minutes, not half an hour, because otherwise we will never be able to complete the proceedings as planned. Having said that, we maintain our decision to give you 50 per cent more time than the Prosecution. We feel that if the questions are properly focussed, that time is quite sufficient. However, should any exceptional circumstances arise, ask permission from us to extend the time, and in the cross-examination that is coming now you will have several documents and then we will understand that the time it takes to produce the document, to hear the opinion of the Prosecution, et cetera, this might justify some extension. For this particular witness, you asked an extra 45 minutes. Let us say that if you put your questions properly, then there will be no need to exceed the time limit. But we will see, depending on the documents that you will be producing, that such an extension may be justified. But we will watch the time with vigilance. To avoid any further wasting of time, we will have the witness brought in immediately. Mr. Usher, would you be kind enough to bring in the witness. It would also be a good idea if you have, five, six, seven documents, before beginning the cross-examination to tell us that you plan to tender five, six, seven documents. That is an indication, and that may not be necessary, but as you have already prepared the cross-examination, you know whether you're going to tender documents or not and you could tell us that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Good day, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning -- good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You spent have the weekend here so that we can continue with your cross-examination. I hope you had a good weekend. I will now let the Defence take the floor. They will commence with the cross-examination. Mrs. Residovic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Chambers. My name is Edina Residovic, and together with my colleague Stephane Bourgon I represent General Hadzihasanovic. We met last week and spoke about the information you had; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Quite right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And similarly, prior to that, you also met Mr. Bourgon on one occasion in London; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And according to your testimony in the course of the examination-in-chief, you were in Bosnia and Herzegovina from September 1993 until April 1994. That was when you were performing your duty in Bosnia. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And during that period of time, if I have understood this correctly, you were in the Department for Military Information, which was part of the UNPROFOR headquarters for Bosnia and Herzegovina. It was in Kiseljak. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your main duties when holding that post consisted of collating military information which you would obtain from various sources. You have also had to assess the information obtained in this manner and forward the information. Was that on the whole your main task?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: That is correct. To assess the information from a variety of sources and information points, to assess it so as to try and predict the future fighting, future warfare and conflict, to allow for the humanitarian aid to pass by the safest route. And I passed those assessments and future assessments to a number of sources, both within and outside Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And as you have said, it was your -- your personal responsibility had to do with the area of the Canadian Battalion, the French Battalion, and the battalion at the airport in Sarajevo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Yes. The -- the British Battalion in the area of Vitez; the Canadian Battalion in the area of Visoko; and French 3rd Battalion in the area of Sarajevo. Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If I have understood this well, the sources you had were the officers, the military information, from these three battalions, liaison officers from the United Kingdom, the European Community Monitoring Mission, and other non-governmental organisations and other organisations; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You would compile a summary of the main information on a weekly basis and send them to the units in the field, to UNPROFOR headquarters in Zagreb, to the UNHCR, and to national intelligence services. This was for the purposes of their government. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Sometimes, as you have testified in the examination-in-chief --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Residovic, I will interrupt you now. The question has already been put, but that wasn't why I was intervening. In line 6, on page 12 you said that the witness passed on his information to the intelligence services, to national intelligence services. That doesn't appear to be what he said in response to the questions put to him by the Prosecution. So I will put the question to you, Witness: The Defence claims that you would compile your reports, which would be forwarded to the UN, the UNHCR, and to intelligence services. This means that you had a direct link with the intelligence services of the various countries that were in the field. Is that the meaning of the question and the meaning of your answer? Because it doesn't appear clear. It didn't appear clear last Friday. What could you tell us about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Each major contributing nation to the United Nations sent back the military information summary and the pictorial information summary that -- those documents that I compiled every Sunday, they would send them back along their national communication chains to their national Ministries of Defence, where the intelligence communities, I would imagine, or assume, the intelligence communities of each national government would then read those summaries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You assume. The question wasn't really in that sense. The question was: Did you have a direct link with the intelligence services? You said it went through the chain of command, it went to the Ministry of Defence Please continue, Mrs. Residovic. The answer wasn't exactly the one that you were thinking of when you put the question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. This question was based on the statement that Mr. Chambers gave to the Prosecution in the course of the investigation, but I think that the witness has clarified the situation when responding to your question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Chambers, as you said, you would sometimes compile subject reports and you spoke about this with the Prosecution on Friday; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: I spoke about it with the Prosecution on Friday in the court, but previously on the Thursday of last week, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: All the information you had, whether these were regular weekly summaries or special subject reports, all -- the main sources for this information were documents that you had previously obtained, either from the battalion -- from battalions in the field or from other organisations; is that correct? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Yes, it is. All the weekly summaries were from the battalions, exactly as you've described. Though occasionally I would be asked to compile a special report on a particular matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So the facts that you presented in the weekly reports and their accuracy depended on the accuracy of the information that you obtained from the field and on the accuracy of the information that you were provided with; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Absolutely correct. I was dependent upon those that reported to me and their reports being accurate, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So if we assume that in -- if in the reports you had the sum of the facts were imprecise or erroneous, these errors would be duplicated in your weekly reports; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Inevitably, yes. There would be occasions where something might be reported in the weekly military information summary that had not been fully substantiated and for which there was no subsequent information, and therefore there may have been inaccuracies within those reports, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In fact, you worked to the best of your ability on the basis of the information that you had at your disposal, but it wasn't your task and it wasn't possible for you either to check the accuracy of the information that you received; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: That is correct. I was not able to verify or substantiate every report, but obviously where possible we tried to connect one, two, or three reports together, and that was as close to substantiation of a report as we could get, correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me, Mr. Chambers, if I said that if you had had other information and more accurate sources, in such a case the conclusions you reached in your weekly reports might have been different?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Of course, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Sometimes in your analysis you would quite simply take over the conclusions or the comments made by battalions in the field and you believed that on the whole this information was accurate and had been verified. Were there such cases?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Generally we believed that the information that was given to us by the battalions and most of our sources of information was accurate in that it had been reported to them or they had seen particular activities. This was not so in every case, of course, but generally the information was accurate as it was reported and from a trusted source. There were, of course, occasions where a single line entry might have been made by a battalion or by a individual but then appeared in the weekly report or weekly information summary just as a line that stood by itself, that did not have any -- necessarily any substantiation. Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Chambers, am I interpreting your answer correctly, the one that you gave to us before this hearing? The information on foreign combatants was received on the whole from individuals, and the source about -- of information about the Mujahedin on the whole was the HVO? Is that what you told us?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: No. What I thought that I told you on Friday and at subsequent meetings -- or on previous meetings with you was that the source of most of the information on the Mujahedin came from the British Battalion and from other sources. The British Battalion themselves may well have received some of that information from the HVO or indeed from some of the ABiH commanders themselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I didn't mean that you personally received this information, but military reporters from the battalion on the whole received this information from individuals. That is what you said; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: The battalion received it from individuals, correct, yes. And the battalion then subsequently reported it to me. Yeah. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You yourself didn't have any official documents that mentioned the existence of the Mujahedin in Central Bosnia; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: If by "official documents" you mean documents belonging to any of the warring factions, no, that is correct. Of course, all the documents that were created by the battalions were official documents, but we had no documents from any of the warring factions, no. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Chambers, was it possible for you to obtain information from various sources, the battalions, international organisations, and the monitors, information that concerned the same event but their conclusions and comments relating to the facts concerned were often divergent? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: The UNPROFOR, United Nations Protection Force, members, United Nations Military Observers, European Community military monitors, and similar organisations, or individuals from those organisations, generally their conclusions to an event were very similar. However, there were divergent views on an event held by each side of the warring factions; that is, HVO and ABiH. But generally those contributing nations for a singular event would hold very similar views as to what had taken place.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Chambers, could you please tell me whether you would agree with what Mr. Williams stated. He testified here last week, and with regard to that problem, he said the following, and I'm quoting; it's page 57, line 8 to 12: "This is an indisputable fact that the information --"

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Withopf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: May I please interrupt at this point in time. I don't find it the appropriate conduct of a cross-examination to make reference to another witness's testimony before this Court. The witness may, for whatever reason, none of the parties know or the Judges may be aware, have a certain connection to certain witnesses, and this reason may influence his answers to the questions put to him. The Prosecution doesn't find it the correct conduct to confront the witness with the testimony of a different witness before this Court in the very same matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mrs. Residovic, what do you have to say about this?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In accordance with the Rules of the Tribunal, with the jurisprudence, I think that in the course of the cross-examination a witness can be presented with all the evidence that has been accepted by this Trial Chamber, all the evidence that has been introduced here. Since General Williams has testified before this Trial Chamber, I think that it is quite appropriate and correct to present part of his testimony or refer to part of his testimony when questioning this witness or any other witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In order to summarise what you have said, you are asking the witness to comment on someone's testimony.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I want to ask the witness whether he would agree with something that the witness Williams stated before this Tribunal. It has to do with the question that I just asked the witness that had to do with contradictory information received from various organisations, the various organisations that were present in the field.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Put your question to the witness, and the Trial Chamber will state its position.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Chambers, I'm going to quote what General Williams said. He testified before this Tribunal and said that the fact that there was contradictory information was something that happened. He said that it was indisputable, that the information obtained from various sources reflected the situation -- presented the situation in various ways and there was also the risk that some people might create a problem by turning rumours into something solid and by repeating these rumours on a number of occasions. My question is whether on the basis of your personal experience you would agree with what this witness stated before the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Indeed. I'm assuming that the Brigadier Williams to whom you refer was at the time Lieutenant Colonel Williams who commanded the Coldstream Guards Battalion in -- British Battalion in Vitez. That being the case, much of the information that I received was from the -- his military information cell, his own staff within his own battalion headquarters. He and his staff were much closer to the warring factions, the HVO, and the ABiH, and consequently they, I am sure, as he has stated, used to hear contradictory versions of events from each side that were engaged in the actual battle. My position, which if you like was one step up in the headquarters, was I would receive more filtered information that had been assessed by his staff and by himself perhaps on occasion and where they would have filtered out some of the excessive claims or each of the warring factions. So the version of events that used to come to me was more filtered and more sanitised, if you like, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, would you nevertheless agree with me if I said that if a rumour was repeated on a number of occasions in a given report, in such cases there was a risk that a certain weight might be attached to such information?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Yes, I would agree. That -- that was always a risk and is still a risk in any military information or intelligence field. That is correct. I can accept that -- that certain weight might be given to information that had been heard two, three, or four times over a period of time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your reports on the Mujahedin and the 7th Muslim Brigade that you sent on the 2nd of November, 1993, was a result of the request made by General Chambers dated the 1st of November 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Given that you received the request by fax on the 1st of November at 11.30 and you replied on the 2nd of November at 15.43, the time you had to compile this report was quite short; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As a result, you based yourself on the report of Captain Whitley [phoen] from the British Army, who was performing his duties in the UNPROFOR command before you arrived; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Not quite. I remember very distinctly the evening of the 1st of November. I sat down and wrote that report - I can clearly remember - in about three hours on the evening of the 1st of November. Based on a number of things, a little bit -- or some on the previous information left by Captain Whitley, a considerable amount based on my own knowledge of the Mujahedin, most of which had been passed to me by the British Battalion in Vitez. So it was, if you like -- again, to use the word, a fusion of information, some of which was in my head, that I had inherited from Captain Whitley, some of which was in reports that had been sent to me by the British Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, you didn't have enough time to check in detail all the information that in the course of 1993 arrived in the command in Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Oh, sorry, that's a question? I did have time. I think, to put it into perspective, as I said before on Friday, this was a -- a quick RFI, request for information, from General Chambers' staff, and they posed me in the facts a number of questions, and those questions I answered, realising that they in Vincenza, the 5th Allied Tactical Air Force, and General Chambers specifically, knew nothing about the Mujahedin and was interested in the background information about who they were, what they were, and what they were doing. Those questions were very specific in the -- in his fax, his staff fax to me, and I answered those questions in the order in which they were presented. And on the pages that you have, the four-page fax in question, you will see underlined the question and then my answer to those specific questions..

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be showed document DH8 [as interpreted]. It's a milinfosum, 32, dated the 31st of May, 1993. DH108, not 8, as it appears in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you have a look under the title "Zenica," item 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Withopf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: A pure technical issue. If the witness would be so polite to put the document on the ELMO, since at the time we don't have the document in front of us.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Chambers, would it be correct to say that in this paragraph you can see that the liaison officer did meet certain Mujahedin, and at the end of this paragraph, paragraph 3, he states that it is his belief that they were not under the control of the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Excuse me. One moment. Yes, it's a poor photocopy, but I can see it. It does say at the bottom "3rd Corps." Yes, I would accept that his belief at that time was they were not under the control of the 3rd Corps. Yes, that's what his statement says.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In item 4 of this milinfosum, you can see that the liaison officer also had a meeting with Commander Jasmin Saric and with another commander. And on page 2 it appears that Commander Saric also gave the impression that the Mujahedin were not under the control of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Yes, I would accept that that seems to be his assessment at that time. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown Defence Exhibit DH72. It is a milinfosum number 46 dated the 14th of June.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This is a milinfosum in which in paragraph 1 it mentions the meeting of a commander from the BritBat with General Hadzihasanovic. And if you have a look at the end of the paragraph - it's the seventh line down - you can see that the deputy commander, Merdan, says that the Mujahedin weren't under the effective control of the 3rd Corps. You can also see that it says that Hadzihasanovic showed a letter he had written and addressed to the Supreme Command in which he requested that the issue, the problem of the Mujahedin, be solved. Is this what this milinfosum states?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Yes, it appears to state that he's seeking the authority of the higher command to -- to, as it puts it in the report, "To deal with what he considered to be a problem," for he, Hadzihasanovic, to deal with what he considered to be a problem. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness also be shown Exhibit DH73, please, dated the 13th of June.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I think you will agree with me if I say that you hadn't seen this document before.

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: That is true. I have not seen this before, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The assessments made in these milinfosums and the document that you saw, had you studied them in detail when you were asked to respond to a fax -- to the fax from General Chambers would probably have affected the position that you presented in your reply. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: This latest document that you have shown me may have had an effect, though I have not read it in detail. The previous milinfosums may not have affected my overall reply to General Chambers in November, which was some five months -- or six months after those milinfosums and some five months after this particular letter, which was the time at which I was writing. But I would accept, again without reading the detail of this yet, that there seems to be -- appears to be a letter to Delic, I think, from Hadzihasanovic. I'm just reading it through now. Yeah. I accept that he at this time appears to be writing to Delic asking for advice as to what to do with the 3rd Corps, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could these two documents be returned now and could the witness be shown Prosecution Exhibit P163 -- actually, the three documents can be returned, and P163 shown to the witness, please. It is a milinfosum dated the 27th of June.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Chambers, would you please look at this milinfosum of the 27th of June, especially the commentary at the end of it.

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Is it this comment here you want --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Is it true that from this comment it is visible that information about foreigners in the 7th Muslim Brigade had come from Commander Nakic from the HVO?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: In this report, it would appear so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Actually, this comment is in a different tone than the earlier documents I showed you because it claims that the Mujahedin are under the control -- are under control; is that right?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: If I can just read for a moment. Yeah, I -- I have to confess I'm slightly confused because I'm not quite sure what he is trying to say here as to whether they are or are not under control. He states: "Should this prove accurate, then all doubts as to whether the Mujahedin are under control or not might be ended." I don't know in which way he means it to be ended. I'm unsure myself. You may be able to enlighten me. Is the confusion "ended" because he considered them to be under control or is the confusion "ended" because he considers them not to be under control?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But the last part of the sentence would appear to mean that the author believes that the 7th Muslim Brigade and the Mujahedin are one and the same. The last sentence of this comment.

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Yeah, that appears to be what he is saying, is that the Mujahedin and 7 Muslim Brigade are one and the same, is what he appears to be saying, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And the source for such a conclusion is Commander Nakic, who was a commander of the Croatian Defence Council. That also follows from this comment, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Again, without reading it, I'm sure that that was the probable source, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Withopf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: It's happened repeatedly that the witness made statements introducing with "without having properly read it," or "without reading it." May my learned friend from the Defence please give the witness sufficient time to actually read the documents which are put in front of him in order to enable to -- to enable him to make an informed statement on the issues he's asked about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Madam Residovic, give the witness time to read, because if you are showing him a document and you want to ask him questions about it, the reply could be amputated from a part of the truth. So will you please rephrase your question, because now he has taken the time to read the document. What you wanted to show was that the source of this information was the HVO; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber fully understands that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do have it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that this comment was made repeatedly in certain reports sent by the British Battalion to the UNPROFOR command regarding the Mujahedin and the 7th Muslim Brigade?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Yes, I think particularly in the early stages - and by that I mean early 1993 - many people used to use -- invitedly use the term "Mujahedin" when referring to the term 7th Muslim Brigade. It was only -- and that was careless by some people and perhaps not sufficiently accurate, because their understanding of the structures at the time were immature. As time went on, I think people began to make the clear distinction between the Mujahedin element and 7 Muslim Brigade and that -- there are two entities maybe within the same body. But early on I accept that the -- the two phrases -- or "7 Muslim Brigade" and "Mujahedin" were almost interchangeable when some people were talking or writing, correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document may be returned now, and could the witness be shown Prosecution Exhibit P376, which is a monitoring daily report dated the 20th of October.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Chambers, could you please read on page 2, paragraph 7.2.

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Yes, I have read that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with me in saying that this report raises the question of control over the Mujahedin and says that this question is still quite open?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Yes, it would appear that the European Community monitor at that time, in this specific instance, felt that they were not under control. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown Prosecution Exhibit P176, which is also a monitor team daily report of the 27th of October, 1993. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would you please look at page 2, paragraph 7, "Comment." And the responses given under a, b, and c. Mr. Chambers, is it clear from this report once again that the army is taking steps and endeavouring to place the Mujahedin under control but that they clearly are not under the control of the Bosnian army?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: It would appear clear that elements of the Mujahedin were not under control or were acting in an independent manner at this stage. That I would accept as being true, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: These reports of the European Monitoring Mission were compiled prior to your report, and had you had access to them, they also could have affected your own report of the 2nd of November; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: It is right in -- in a general sense, but I note this particular report was published only three days before the request for information from General Chambers. I used to read all of these reports from the European Commission Military Monitors that used to get passed to me. Indeed, I may have read this particular report at that time. I can't say. So would it have -- your question was: Would it have possibly affected my answer to General Chambers in my response. I may have had this information already in my head; I may not. I don't believe that it would have -- this particular small piece would have over -- would have changed my overall message that I was giving back to General Chambers, though I accept this is a -- a small piece of a big picture.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness now be shown Prosecution Exhibit P181. It is a report of the European monitors, the regional centre in Zenica, dated the 3rd of November, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at page 2, paragraph 10.

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: There's a paragraph 10 on page 8, here. It starts --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: "When asked whether he was --" "When asked about the..." Yes, I've read that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that it would follow from this report that at a meeting held with the deputy commander of the 3rd Corps, the deputy commander made it clear that the Mujahedin were not under control and that there were efforts either to send them back to their own countries or to place them under control and that there were also other groups that called themselves Mujahedin but who are in fact not foreign fighters? Would that briefly be what emerges from this paragraph 10?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Yes. Though I think we have been using the word "control" for some time, you and myself. I think we perhaps ought to define our understanding -- our mutual understanding of the term "control." Seeing this as a distinct control in a discipline -- in a disciplinary way, as opposed to command. And the two are slightly separate. And you may wish to speak about that or question me on that later, which is fine. In the strict sense of word "control," were they able to be held in check or held in control, I accept that there were individuals who were not able to be controlled and were not held in check because they lacked the discipline or whatever. That, I accept, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So you do accept that Enver Hadzihasanovic at this meeting made it quite clear that foreigners were a problem which they were trying to deal with, either by sending them away from Bosnia and Herzegovina or by having them integrated within the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, indeed. But I thought the meeting was between the political advisor, Commander Merdan.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In the first part, it refers to a meeting with Mr. Merdan, but on page 7 you will see that it continues with a conversation with Enver Hadzihasanovic, the commander of the 3rd Corps of the BH army, and this paragraph refers to that meeting.

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Withopf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: This manner to ask the witness questions about these documents appears to be a bit problematic, since my learned friend from the Hadzihasanovic Defence does nothing else than making the witness paraphrasing what's written in the document. The witness himself was not at any of the meetings in which these things have been said, so how can the witness comment beyond what's actually said in the document and in answering the questions by my learned friend? This appears to be problematic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, may I respond? On Friday, the witness explained his assignment and role, and he said that he received all the information and that he analysed this document. He confirmed that in answer to a question from me. Therefore, the witness is a person who cannot testify about facts, but he can provide an analysis of the documents which were sent to him. And it is for these reasons I am showing the witness documents which he must have received at the UNPROFOR command in Kiseljak and which he probably commented on in his reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But the question regarding the last document -- Witness, the document you have in front of you, have you seen it? Do you remember having seen this particular document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I -- with virtually every document, sir, I can't specifically remember this document; however, I almost certainly would have received this document, and that being the case would have almost certainly read that document, now, 11 years ago. I cannot absolutely say that I have read this document before, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We take note of your answer. I'm going to interrupt you because it is almost time for us to take the break. We will resume at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We will now resume. The Trial Chamber would like to ask you to forgive us for being a little late. Within the framework of the questions put to the witness, we'd like to ask the Defence to proceed rapidly. And could you try to avoid asking questions that have already been put. We have noticed that the witness has already answered some of the questions put to him. In addition, there is a slight mystery in that we don't know whether the Defence team for Mr. Kubura will also take up a certain amount of time for the cross-examination of the witness. So, Mr. Dixon, do you intend to cross-examine the witness or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we do. We don't have too many questions. At the maximum, 30 to 40 minutes, at the extreme end of the scale.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mrs. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I am halfway through my cross-examination. I would like to inform the Trial Chamber that I would like to show the witness four Prosecution exhibits which refer to the same things that he has informed Mr. Chambers of. I would also like to tender five other documents, five new documents. So I would like to ask the Trial Chamber to allow me to continue with my cross-examination. Could the witness now be shown Exhibit 379, Prosecution Exhibit 379. This is a letter from General Williams to the UNPROFOR command dated the 5th of December, 1993, and there are certain attachments too.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Chambers, would you first have a look at the letter from Captain Guinness dated the 26th of November. Have a look at paragraph 2, the last sentence in paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Yes, I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This seems to show that Captain Guinness claimed on the 26th of November that the Mujahedin were not under control. Is that what this document states?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: It appears to state that some elements are out of control, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you have a look at the letter that the then-colonel, now a general, Williams sent to Brigadier Ramsay. Have a look at page 1, paragraph 1, the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Yes, understood.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This document also shows that it is quite unclear whether the Mujahedin are under the control -- were under the control of the 3rd Corps. Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Yes. Again, if I might just mention the issue of control and command. I fully accept that there are elements of the Mujahedin who were out of control, who were operating perhaps outside of the norms of any command structure, yes. But the issue of command is a separate issue perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification. If necessary, as you have said, it's an issue we can go back to.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could Mr. Chambers now be shown a document from the regional centre of the ECMM dated the 29th of December -- the 18th of December, 1993. We have a sufficient number of copies to distribute to everyone in the courtroom and to our colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Chambers, would you please have a look at the heading, the "15th of December." It's on page 5, dated the 15th of December. It's paragraph 2 that I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Is it the -- the one that starts, "The white road convoy..."

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: No. You've been given a weekly report dated the 18th of December; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: On page 5, under the date the 15th of December, item 2 states that, "The liaison officer of the operations group Bosnian Krajina..."

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: I now have it. I'm reading it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This report also seems to show that the liaison officer from Bosnian Krajina informed you that the Mujahedin were out of control; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Yes, it appears that this report says that. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Given that the document is dated the 18th of December and it's a document from the Central Bosnia area, I suggest that this document be admitted into evidence. We received it from the Prosecution on the disk that Mr. Chambers provided the Prosecution with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Withopf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, it may be a technical issue only, but the question was: This report also seems to show that the liaison officer from Bosnian Krajina informed you - informed you - that the Mujahedin were out of control. That's the understanding of the Prosecution that the witness did not himself talk to the liaison officer of the ops group Bosanska Krajina, at least not at the time when this report was compiled. It may be just an issue of the transcript. And if I may please ask my learned friend from the Hadzihasanovic Defence to clarify this issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you. I was only stating that the information that the witness received from the liaison officer from the OG Bosnian Krajina stated that the Mujahedin were out of control and this weekly report dated the 18th of December is a document that the witness provided the OTP with.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this exhibit into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Withopf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar, could we have a number for the document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The exhibit number is DH130.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness now be shown a report dated the 29th of December, 1993. It's from the regional centre in Zenica of the European monitors. We have a sufficient number of copies for everyone here.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Chambers, have a look at page -- the page numbered ZA00772 and have a look at item e.

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Yes, I've read that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me if I said that Commander Alagic quite clearly stated here that the Mujahedin were out of control and that they had been asked to respect the laws of the country and to join the BH army; otherwise, they would be treated as paramilitary units? Is this what is stated in the report?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: That appears to be so, and that he had taken certain measures regarding some Mujahedin units who had now left Zenica. That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, since this is an ECMM document, we suggest that for the time being the document only be marked for identification and we will try to tender the document into evidence when we have a representative from the ECMM as a witness here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Withopf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, again, no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this document be marked for identification, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: DH131 ID, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Chambers, would it be correct to say that the report that I have shown to you and they preceded the report you forwarded to General Chambers as well as the ones that were forwarded subsequently, these reports show that there was a problem as far as controlling the Mujahedin were concerned and show that they weren't under the control of the 3rd Corps? Will you agree with this conclusion?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: I certainly agree that there was a problem with certain elements of the Mujahedin and that they -- shall we call them rogue elements that may have carried out some independent actions and were beyond the norms of control as we understand it, though the -- again, I come back to the issue of control and command and to make the differentiation between whether or not a grouping - say, some of the Mujahedin - felt they were under command of a higher authority or whether there were some elements, which I believe there were, that believed themselves to be independent of any norms of military command.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Chambers, could you confirm that when performing your duties you received a number of reports from the BritBat but also from other international organisations and these reports stated that conflicts arose between the Mujahedin and members of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: That is true, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You were also aware of the fact that the Mujahedin carried out an armed attack against the commander of the 7th Muslim Brigade, against Amir Kubura? Were you aware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: No, I wasn't. No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know that the Mujahedin also attacked some members of the 17th Krajina Brigade?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: I was aware of frictions between the 17th Krajina Brigade and 7 Muslim Brigade, and in particular I'm aware of a threat by the commander of 17th Krajina Brigade to lay down mortar fire upon one of the commanders within 7 Muslim Brigade by the name of Abu Haris, who commanded a company of Mujahedin in the area of Mehurici. So yes, I -- I am aware of frictions that in some cases led to threats of hostile acts.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please, could you tell me whether you would agree with me if I said that the commander concerned was Commander Cuskic and he is the one who threatened the Mujahedin in Mehurici? It wasn't the 17th -- it wasn't the 7th Muslim Brigade.

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: The commander to whom I'm referring may well have been the name Commander Cuskic, but I believe him to have been the commander of 17 Brigade at the time, and his threat was to the commander known as Abu Haris who commanded the majority of the foreign national Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also received information according to which a conflict broke out between the Bosniak population in the territory of the 3rd Corps and the Mujahedin, referred to in the ECMM reports. Were you aware of such information?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: I cannot remember a specific event. I am, however, aware that the Mujahedin were very unpopular with the local population because of their significant fundamentalist views and indeed some of their behaviour. Yes, I'm aware that they -- there was friction between the Mujahedin and the local population.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Nevertheless the knowledge you had about conflicts that broke out with the army brigades and the Mujahedin and the knowledge you had about the dissatisfaction of the population with the Mujahedin is not information that you included in the report that you forwarded to General Chambers; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: In fact, I think in my report I did actually say that the Mujahedin were unpopular with the local population. I think I used those or similar words. I also think I may have made mention in that four-page fax to which we all refer to there being frictions within the Bosnian army.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have indirectly checked this. That's what you said; although, you didn't specifically mention the 17th Krajina Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like the witness to be shown Exhibit P223. This is a report dated the 2nd of November forwarded by this witness at the request of General Chambers.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You do remember this report, so I'll ask you my question: Would it be correct to say that in item 1 of this reply you say that you have attached a graphic representation of ORBAT and according to the latest information it represents the command structure of the 7th Muslim Brigade? Is that what your report states?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I'd now like to talk about the information provided in the attachment, in the graphic representation attached.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness also be shown P123.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The document I am showing to you is an order concerning the establishment of the 3rd Corps, dated the 19th of November, 1992; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: It appears so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Chambers, could you very quickly have a look at items 111, 112, et cetera, at the place names that define the zone of responsibility of the 3rd Corps. The last number is 113.

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Yes. I've got a general idea, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that in this order no mention is made anywhere of Maglaj as an area covered by the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: I will accept that, yeah, without reading it in detail. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that in responding to questions from my learned friend you said that whatever is written within these boxes are verified facts?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Yes. I said -- I said in response to the Prosecution's question that where information was known and was a known fact, it was written below the boxes or in numbers to the left and right of the box. So yes, where information is not known, it was left as a blank.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: On your table, it appears that the 7th Muslim Brigade was also deployed in Maglaj, because we see the word "Maglaj" beneath the box. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: It is correct, and therefore that would have been a fact. But I also remember on Friday, when responding to your learned friend, the Prosecution, to say that Maglaj at that time was a pocket that was cut off and was not visited by UNPROFOR troops, and therefore information was very scant about the Maglaj pocket, as we called it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So this fact appearing on your table is one that you cannot claim with certainty that it is correct.

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: That is correct, yes. I cannot absolutely certainly say that there was a battalion -- the 4th Battalion of the 7th Brigade in Maglaj.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the column when you talk about the command structure, beneath the word "Travnik" there's the name of the commander of the 1st Battalion, Assim Korcic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: That's what the chart would say, yes. I cannot actually remember if he was the commander at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: According to your answer given to the Prosecution, that would have to be a known fact; isn't that right? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Correct. Correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness now be shown a list of the officers of the Brigade Staff and officers working in the premises of the school dated the 12th of January, 1993. It's a document of the 7th Muslim Brigade, and we received it from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This is a document dated the 12th of January, 1993, and as you can see, under "1" it is indicated that Koricic Asim was commander of the 7th Muslim Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Does that follow from this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Withopf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object to this line of questioning for two reasons: The name that is mentioned on Prosecution Exhibit P123 isn't Assim Korcic. It's certainly not the name which is mentioned on the document which has now been shown to the witness dated the 12th of January, 1993. And even if there would be a difference between the two documents, I wish to emphasise that the one document of 12th of January, 1993 reflects the situation of 12th of January, 1993; whereas, the other document reflects the situation certainly later on during the year 1993. For these two obvious reasons, I object that the witness is asked such line of questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Can the Defence address the point raised by the Prosecution, who are contesting that document P123 bears the name "Koricic."

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it is one and the same person that the Prosecutor is aware of and who was at the beginning the commander of the 7th Muslim Brigade, before Amir Kubura took over that post. As the witness responding to questions from the Prosecution said that these were known facts and that they applied to the 2nd of November, my next question to the witness is whether he ever received any information or document confirming that Assim Korcic became a battalion commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Withopf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, it's certainly true that the Prosecution is aware that a certain Assim Korcic was the 7th Muslim Brigade commander at a point in time, but the document which my learned friend is referring to, there is a different name. It says, "Assim Korcic," and we are not talking about the commander of the 7th Muslim Brigade but about the commander of the 1st Battalion of the 7th Muslim Brigade, what's obviously a difference. I also wish to draw the attention of the Trial Chamber that the document which the Defence is currently using in showing the witness is a document which stems from the Prosecution and which the Defence has contested. It's on the contested exhibit list, what appears to be quite strange.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, you know that the Defence has contested documents for various reasons, the main reason being that we wish to check the contents of certain documents through witnesses. I do not expect this witness to recognise this document, but the witness said that the facts contained in these boxes were verified facts as of the date of the report, and we wish to indicate that at the time the witness did not have the real facts at his disposal. That is what the Defence would like to show. And I think that the witness himself said at the beginning that had he had different information, then his conclusions would probably have been different as well. That is what the witness himself said. My question to the witness now is:

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you, Mr. Chambers, ever receive a document from which it would follow that the former commander at the 7th Muslim Brigade at some point in time became battalion commander in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Withopf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object against this question, since the name on the document which has been produced by the witness is apparently different from the name which is on the 12th of January, 1993 document; and in addition, Defence has objected to the Prosecution tendering the 12th of January, 1993 document into evidence for the reason that it's outside the relevant time frame for the indictment. The Defence appears to contradict themselves at this point in time. Either it can be used or it can't be used. And the main reason, however, is that the two names on the two different documents are obviously different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. In the document P223, under "Travnik, Commander Assim Korcic" it says. That is the question you're asking, isn't it? And to show that the indication that he was the commander of the 7th Brigade would be in contradiction with the fact that in P223 the name of that -- he is the commander in Travnik. Will you please explain your question, because we are having some difficulty in following you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, according to the indictment itself, the 1st Command of the 7th Muslim Brigade was Assim Korcic, who after that left, and as of April Amir Kubura became the commander, according to the indictment. There is a letter, one "I" is missing, but to say that that same person was in November commander of a battalion is a fact which has been put on the chart because probably the witness had incorrect data about the names of battalion commanders in the 7th Muslim Brigade, and that is my question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Withopf, I'm going to give you the floor. But the question is a very simple one: Witness, we have a document and a list of officers of the 7th Brigade. This document is dated the 12th of January, 1993, and number 1 is Assim Korcic. And then in the document that you prepared in November, which means several months prior to this one, we have indicated that a battalion commander - that is a level below - Assim Korcic. So there's a big question there. The document that you drafted in November, does it not contain a colossal error, since Mr. Assim Korcic would have been demoted and would be a battalion commander in Travnik; whereas, in the document that you have in front of you he's number 1? What explanation are you giving for that? If it is the same person, of course. The question the Defence is putting to you would mean that in your document you're referring to the same person. According to you, is it the same person or are we talking about two different people? Because if it is the same person, we have a problem. And if they are two different persons, then there's no problem. What are you telling us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know, sir, is the answer. All I'm aware of is the new document I have been produced here, showing Assim Korcic as the brigade commander in January of 1993, 11 months later it was Kubura who was the commander. What happened to Koricic I don't know. The chart shows an "Assim Korcic." Whether it is the same man or not, I don't know. I agree with you, though, sir, it would be unlikely for the brigade commander to be demoted down to battalion commander 11 months later, but I don't know if it is the same man or not, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Chambers, if I were to tell you or if you had the documents which would indicate that the command of the 2nd Battalion in Zenica was never Hidan Kisanovic [phoen], but Serif Patkovic and that the commander of the 3rd Battalion in Kakanj, Nihad Catic, stopped being the commander of that battalion in June 1993, had you had such documents then what you wrote down would not correspond to the actual state of affairs, would it?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Withopf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, my learned friend from the Hadzihasanovic Defence tries to make the witness speculate, and this can certainly be not the purpose of the testimony of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Defence is making submissions which it will seek to prove during its case. The witness told us that he drafted reports and charts on the basis of the knowledge he had at the time. Since he made an assessment to the effect that his report could have been different had the information been different, I am asking him if he had known these facts would this chart, then, have been in the same way as it is now. Would it have been different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll give you the floor, Mr. Withopf. The question is quite a simple one, in fact: Hypothetically, if Assim Korcic is one and the same, in November when you prepared your chart, would you have said the same thing or would you have changed your chart? If, of course, it is the same person. If they are two different people, then it's another matter. So the attorney is telling you if you had this list and if you had seen that Koricic was number 1, would you have indicated on your chart that he was battalion commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably not, sir. But if I can clarify, which may help the Court; it may not. The -- the issue that you are asking, it would appear to me, is whether what is printed on the chart was an absolute 100 per cent fact in every case on the day that this was printed. My answer should you have asked me that was the -- where we place names, places, and numbers on these charts means that we have substantiated those facts at some point in time. Obviously these facts change, and often. Units move; commanders change.
