Therefore, on that specific day, there may have been changes that had happened within the ABiH structure, maybe in some cases one or two months before, which had not yet been relayed -- the information had not come to us, and so therefore the chart -- it was not known to us, and therefore there may be old information that is contained on these charts, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Also, Mr. Chambers --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think Mr. Withopf had something to say, but he sat down. What was it you wanted to say, Mr. Withopf? I asked you to wait for the answer of the witness before giving you the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The witness has actually clarified the issue I wanted to address.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Chambers, you did not have occasion to see an order on the formation of the 7th Muslim Brigade, did you?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If I were to put it to you that the 7th Muslim Brigade pursuant to that order had only three battalions, then the chart indicating a fourth battalion under the 7th Muslim Brigade would not be in line with the actual structure of the 7th Muslim Brigade, would it?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: That is correct. Though I think you have probably drawn attention to note 4 about the Maglaj brigade, which says under note 4: "Probably no longer in the Maglaj area."

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, you would agree with me if I say that the information that the 7th Muslim Brigade had four battalion [as interpreted] would not correspond to the facts?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Yes, I would accept that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In your report, you say that the 7th Muslim Brigade was the only manoeuvre brigade; is that right?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: No. I'm not -- that is not the case, in that manoeuvre brigades, by my understanding, are brigades that are able to manoeuvre in offence, defence, or whatever military operation you are conducting. Obviously the ABiH had a number of manoeuvre brigades. I did, however, say that they were their predominant manoeuvre brigade who used to be used as the "schwerpunkt," i.e., the point of attack more often than not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Residovic, the Chamber is wondering whether the Defence counsel for Mr. Kubura, whether Mr. Dixon might not wish to ask the witness a question regarding this point, because in the document the 7th Brigade is under the command of Mr. Kubura in Travnik as head of battalion, Mr. Assim Korcic. Mr. Dixon, would you like to intervene at this point?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would prefer to keep all my questions together at the end, after Mrs. Residovic has finished. This is certainly a point that I did wish to ask the witness a few questions on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I wasn't seeing you, so the Chamber wanted to have a clear view.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Chambers, in this chart, in one of the boxes you said that an 8th Muslim Brigade had been formed, and it says, "Zenica Mehurici," but next to the name there's a question mark. That means that you had information that the 8th Brigade had been formed but you didn't know its name. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Yes. At that time, we had heard rumours, discussion of the possibility of a -- an 8th Muslim Brigade. We did not know its name, hence the question mark, and the -- the grid reference, Zenica-Mehurici there was assumed to be where the headquarters would form -- was formed up. I have to confess I do not know -- I cannot remember whether 8th Muslim Brigade had formed at this point or whether they were still in formation. I suspect it was the latter; they were still forming at this time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, in your testimony, in response to questions from the Prosecution, you said that the brigade consisted exclusively of foreign fighters; is that right?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: No., that is not right. I very clearly stated, and I think in testimony, and indeed on this fax, that the brigade consisted of between five and 800 fighters of which approximately 200 or so, two to 300 were Mujahedin and that the other elements of the brigade were either fundamentalist Muslims - national, not -- by that I mean Bosnian, as opposed to foreign - so not in the slightest did I ever infer that 7 Muslim Brigade was exclusively foreign fighters, never.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I must have phrased my question wrongly. So we didn't understand one another. I was asking you about the 8th Muslim Brigade, because it says under number 3 that you believed that the new 8th Muslim Brigade consisted exclusively of foreigners. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Yes. I -- I believe that the intention of the Bosnian army was to try and force - and I use the word fairly advisedly - force the Mujahedin into one formed unit under 8th Muslim Brigade and bring all Mujahedin together under -- under that one unit to be known as 8 Brigade, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Residovic, we are making our calculations, and you have already used up two hours. How much more time do you need? Because as Mr. Dixon told us, he would need 30 minutes, we are going to exceed the time limit. What are the exceptional reasons for which you need more time?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I am close to the end, but I think I would need another 15 minutes or so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you any more documents? You need 15 documents [as interpreted] -- do you have any new documents or not? You need 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have two documents. And a Prosecution document that has already been admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You will be able to continue, but I'm going to ask the witness for a point of clarification. As we're talking about the 8th Brigade, in the chart where it says, "El Mujahed" with a question mark, there's the square, "Zenica-Mehurici," and below that it says, "YJ 10.205." What does that mean? What does that mean, those numbers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is the grid reference, i.e., the map reference, the point on the map at where their -- where their headquarters was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. Madam Residovic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is my understanding correct, Mr. Chambers, that you just said that there were certain indications that the 8th Muslim Brigade was in formation? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Which means that your report -- your reports could have contained certain possible facts and not only the facts that you were quite certain about.

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: In the case of 8 Muslim Brigade, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like the witness to be shown milinfosum number 156, dated the 1st of October, and the report of the 24th of October of the UNPROFOR command in Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Residovic, on the list that you produced, what do you wish to do with this document? Are you going to ask that it be tendered? Are you going to withdraw it?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. I withdraw that document. We will be discussing it when we have the discussion about documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Withopf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, I find this procedure a bit unusual. The Defence shows the witness a document, a document which they got from the Prosecution. It's a document Defence has objected to and contested, and the reasons are outlined in their filing on the contested documents. They used this document in order to ask the witness a number of questions, and once they are asked, whether they wish to tender it or to mark it for identification, the answer is, "We will discuss this document once we have the court sessions on the documents." This procedure isn't a fair procedure under any circumstances. Either the Defence contests a document, meaning that they don't use it, or they accept it as a Prosecution exhibit. But to ask the witness to comment on the document and later on to contest it appears to be a bit unusual.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, if my learned colleague has no objections to this document - I thought that he did have an objection - in order not to waste time, the Defence would like to suggest that this exhibit be admitted into evidence, the document about the office structure of the 7th Muslim Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber will withdraw for a few minutes and we will be back in a few minutes' time. --- Break taken at 5.17 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With regard to the document, the list from the 7th Brigade containing the names of officers, the Defence would like to tender the document into evidence. No objections have been raised by the Prosecution, so I would like to ask Madam Registrar to give us an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Is DH132, and the English translation, DH132/E.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Having given the document number DH132 for the B/C/S version and for the English version DH132/E, the Trial Chamber has admitted this document into evidence now, but nevertheless the Trial Chamber would like to point out that the Defence has proceeded strangely. You first of all contested the document and then you requested that it be admitted into evidence, so there's something that's not quite coherent here. Nevertheless, we understand the fact that this is a useful document. When you contested the document, perhaps you didn't realise the interest it had. Secondly, as far as the time you have taken up is concerned, you have used up more time allocated to you, we would like you to respect the amount of time allocated to you. We have to control the time that both parties use up, because otherwise the Prosecution could also take up a lot of time when conducting its examination-in-chief. And since the Defence has another 50 per cent of time when cross-examining, well, we might have to spend another day to examine a witness. So we have to restrict the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. amount of time used up by the Prosecution, and you should do so as well. When you are putting questions to witnesses, you must bear in mind the fact that the Judges are listening to the questions. There is no jury here; there are professional Judges sitting in the courtroom who can immediately assess the scope of the questions and the value of the answers provided. This is why you have to go to what is essential immediate.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Chambers, could you have a look at the milinfosum dated the 21st of October, under b. Is it correct to say it that says the 8th El Mujahed Brigade was established and it consisted of local and foreign combatants? It's milinfosum number 156, dated the 1st of October.

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Yes, I have the same. Yes, it -- it does say that it had formed, and the information is contained, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So this is contrary to what you stated in the graphic representation, according to which this brigade was composed of foreigners alone; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Yes. Except that you will note the date of the milinfosum 156 is dated 1st of October. I would have received this report on the morning of the 2nd of October, having written my report, which we discussed, on the evening of the 1st. So actually, this is new information which came immediately subsequent to my fax that went to General Chambers in Vincenza.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you have a look at the report dated the 24th of October, have a look at item -- the item -- or the heading "Warring parties." Have a look at b.

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Yeah, I'm looking at it. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the sixth line, doubt is still expressed as to whether the 8th Muslim Brigade had been formed; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Yes, it appears that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So this report, dated the 1st of October, and the one dated 24th of October, compiled before your report dated the 2nd of November -- or in fact, dated the 30th of October and the 2nd of November, they contained facts that don't reflect the facts in your graphic representation -- or rather, they represent these facts in a slightly -- or in a different light. Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Very slightly, yes. I -- I still believe that the graphic representation of 8 Muslim Brigade was correct at the time of writing on the graph and was then further substantiated by the written reports that you have here, either before or after that fax. What it may not have included was the line that you drew out, that it may contain some national elements, not just foreigners, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown P378.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This is a report that concerns the organisation of the 3rd and the 6th Corps. Please have a look at item 15.

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Yes, understood.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If I remind you of the document dated the 27th of June, a milinfosum which contains a comment on the Mujahedin in the 7th Muslim Brigade, and it's a document compiled on the basis of information from Commander Nakic, an HVO commander, would you agree with me if I said that item 15 adopted the comment contained in the milinfosum dated the 27th of June?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: What, do you mean that the -- there are some members who dress as though they are 7 Muslim Brigade? Is that the point you're making?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Yes, I accept that that may well have been happening, yes, from these reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So you agree that some comments were simply copied into other reports and they didn't take into account all the documents and the facts concerning the composition of the 7th Muslim Brigade and the Mujahedin that we have referred to today in this courtroom?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: I fully accept that many comments are copied from one report to another report without any further substantiation by the author at the higher levels of our command, because we are not able, or were not able, to substantiate them -- any of them all [sic]. That is not a problem to me to say, yes, that certain parts, certain reports were copied across into another report, to make the formation of another report.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And finally, Mr. Chambers -- and finally, Mr. Chambers, would you agree with me if I said that at the end of your duties in the UNPROFOR command in Kiseljak you were not in a position to have a clear idea of the Mujahedin and you cannot confirm that they were part of the 7th Brigade or under the command of the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: The answer to that is potentially very long and which we have discussed before, and I think the -- I think I did have as good a picture as anybody else in UNPROFOR at that time. But as I'm sure you will have heard other witnesses in this Court say, perhaps, that we were observers in somebody else's war; we were not fighting the war ourselves. Consequently our focus and our intensity for divining the information about what the warring factions were doing to one another was perhaps not as intense as if we had been fighting the war ourselves. I did, however, have probably as good an overview of the Mujahedin as anybody else, and I would also state that the business about control and command is still an issue that -- that I think is open in my mind. I believe that there are elements that were no longer under control and were operating as mavericks, but I do believe that -- that there was a command structure and it was our belief, our perception at the time that, 7 Muslim Brigade fell within the operating area of 3rd Corps and consequently 3rd Corps had administrative and logistical responsibility for 7 Muslim Brigade, though they may not have had the operational control of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And finally, am I interpreting your very graphic answer when you said that you sometimes felt that you were faced with a sort of curtain that you would attach certain pictures to, you thought they were accurate, but when the curtain was opened, you realised that reality was quite often different? Have I correctly interpreted what you said?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: You have correctly interpreted an analogy I have made before, and it is so of any war: If you are looking at the war through a curtain, or at a curtain, there are certain chinks or small pieces of light and you make up the picture as you see it. Obviously when the curtain is drawn back and, 11 years on, other documents and other history and other testimony comes to light, the picture may not have been exactly as you were seeing it at the time. That is accepted in all wars in any intelligence community. That is without a doubt. So you make the best picture you have at the time. History may well prove you wrong or that the picture was different.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel Chambers.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I would just like to ask that the last two documents that I showed the witness be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You are requesting that milinfosum 156 be admitted into evidence, dated the 1st of October, 1993; as well as the document from the UNPROFOR -- the UNPROFOR document that concerns the implementation of the peace plan in Bosnia and Herzegovina. You are also requesting that this be admitted into evidence; is that correct? Mr. Withopf, these are two official documents that we have.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The milinfosum number 156 dated the 1st of October, 1993, DH133; and the operations order, implementation of peace plan in Bosnia and Herzegovina dated 24 October, 1993, is Exhibit Number DH134.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would like to thank you for allowing us to conclude our cross-examination of the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. It's 25 to 6.00 now. We have to have our second break. We will resume at 6.00 and we will have one hour exactly. Mr. Dixon has told us that he will take 30 minutes for his cross-examination, perhaps even less. I know how concise Mr. Dixon can be, so it will certainly be less. And then Mr. Withopf, who can also be very concise, will proceed. And if any time is left, the Judges will also ask some questions. We will resume at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dixon, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Colonel Chambers, would it be correct to say that only on rare occasions did the UN sources gather information from what they had seen, as opposed to what they had heard?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Yes, that would be entirely true.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: And that applied to you as well, as a person in the field?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Even more so to me. I -- I didn't go out an awful lot, so I relied mainly on reports and reported speech, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: And the information as we've heard was being obtained from hearing from the warring sides and hearing from locals on the ground.

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: A lot of that information, yes, was -- was gathered that way, from local people, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: One of the ways in which the UN gathered information was by driving around in a UN vehicle handing out cigarettes and sljivovica in exchange for information; is that right?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Yes, particularly with the United Kingdom liaison officers, with the warring faction commanders would sit, have sljivovica, give cigarettes, and, if you like, in part -- in conversation, whilst smoking the cigarettes and the coffee, sljivovica they would receive information, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: And they were also offered to local persons in villages when travelling around in order to obtain information?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Possibly less so in that case, but I'm sure that that would have happened, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: You would agree with me that what you don't see with your own eyes is partially true?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: I would agree with you that you're entirely dependent upon the integrity of the person that is telling you the information, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: And where that information is inaccurate, then it will end up in a report and remain inaccurate. You've confirmed that already.

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Yes, that did inevitably happen, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Your role consisted of hearing, as we've outlined, information from various sources, summarising it, and forming perceptions of what was occurring on the ground.

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Yes, that's -- that's correct. I was to build up an overall picture, a perception of movement, potential attacks, potential pressures, and so on if. It was -- yes, to create an overwash, an overview of what was going on, rather than detailed specifics.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: And in connection with the specific allegation that appears in your report that approximately 200 foreigners, Mujahedin, were located in the 7th Brigade, that was a perception of yours, as you've described the term now?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Yes. It would have been from a report, again from British Battalion, from a variety of sources over a period of time that would have led to that figure, and indeed to where they thought they fitted in the command structure of the ABiH, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: But you have no hard evidence that they were incorporated into the structure of the 7th Brigade, do you?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: I have no paperwork or hard evidence to -- to support that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: You have said that you were aware that a person by the name of Mr. Abu Haris, a foreigner, commanded the majority of the foreign Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: That is correct. And the name Abu Haris is phonetic. We never had, as far as I'm aware, the -- necessarily the correct spelling of his name. But he did command the majority of the Mujahedin and was based in Mehurici, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: You've also said that there was a disaffected group of foreigners who came to fight for a holy war, but that they did not find a place in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Rather than specifically a -- a place on the map --

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: At home. I correct myself.

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Indeed. Yes. They -- I think they were disillusioned because they felt that they had come there to fight Jihad, a holy war, and that is not what they found when they arrived, and consequently they were disaffected, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: And you've said that these elements that we've referred to now could have been a group apart from the 7th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: That is very difficult to know. I don't know the -- the absolute answer to that. As to how many Mujahedin were with Abu Haris and whether there were other smaller groupings, say, who were set apart, I -- I don't actually know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Yes, you've said that there was a time when 7th Brigade was synonymous with Mujahedin. That was earlier on. But then understandings crystallised and they were then seen as two entities. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Indeed, what I was trying to -- to impart was that, I think, people commonly confused the term "Mujahedin" with 7 Muslim Brigade. However, those who studied, if you like, like myself in more detail realised there were two separate entities within the same body. The Mujahedin element, predominantly under Abu Haris, and then, if you like, the national Bosnian element within 7 Muslim Brigade, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Would it be correct to say that the situation regarding the command structure of the Mujahedin was at best grey?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Yes, I think that is entirely fair to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: If you had been fighting in the war yourself, it's likely that that information would have been obtained through proper intelligence sources. But as you've said, you were not involved in the war.

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: I think that is entirely fair. We would have -- (a), we would have had the resources and would have gone out of our way to define and develop our greater understanding of the Mujahedin, 7 Muslim Brigade, and indeed all warring factions. We didn't have the resources, in terms of physically seeing who was where, and therefore we were reliant predominantly upon third party reports. If it had been our own war, yes, we would have given more resources to that particular problem and would have put in a lot more energy to finding out more, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you. On the preparation of your report, you indicated that you prepared it in the course of one evening. There was some urgency about getting it off, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: I really prepared it that evening out of my own convenience, I seem to remember. Most evenings were quiet, where I did most of my analysis. This report had come in, and I answered it there and then over a period of about three hours of typing and a bit of research to get it back the next day just to clear my desk, as much as anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Yes. You never at that time, when you were preparing your report, you never went out into the field to conduct any further research or any further interviews, did you?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: You say that it was based largely on your own information that you had and a little bit from Captain Whitley's report; is that right?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Yes, and virtually all of it, if you like, was not things that I had seen of my own eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: But reports that were given to me. But predominantly from the British Battalion reports in whose area 7 Muslim Brigade lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: So that would have been things that you had heard after you arrived in September 1993.

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: You were obviously not there in June or July 1993.

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Captain Whitley's report was also a general impression report. You said it was a short report. Was it one which was also in the form of an overview?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Yes. I think it was a -- on memory, it was a report that had been built up over a period of time since the British had been in theatre and was a fusion of lots of little elements that had come together and gave an overview of what he, at that time, believed was the command structure and the size, scale of the Mujahedin and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: You didn't go month by month reporting on what the situation was, did you?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: I don't believe Captain Whitley did, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: At the time when you prepared the report, you had not met Mr. Amir Kubura, who was at that time the commander of the 7th Brigade, had you?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: I did not meet him then, and I had not met him until I arrived in this courtroom today.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Did you know that he was the acting commander of the 7th Brigade from the 1st of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: I -- I did not, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: That he was standing in for Mr. Assim Korcic who remained as the commander until August 1993?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: I was not aware of that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: You had never been to the headquarters of the 7th Brigade in Zenica, had you?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: I did not, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: You didn't know where the headquarters were located.

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: I think it had been pointed out to me, but I never visited.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: You didn't have a list of members of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Not a -- an ABiH list.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Obviously we had the British Battalion list of what they thought it consisted of and the personalities within it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: You didn't have any 7th Brigade documents or orders, did you?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: You did say in your report - I don't know if you have it in front of you there; I'm sure you do -- you don't. It's been taken away.

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: It doesn't matter. I can -- I know it very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Perhaps we can try and do it for the purposes of moving through it quickly, without your referring to the report, that the 7th Brigade were grouped under the command of the 3rd Corps and that certainly the 3rd Corps command gives operational direction. Do you recall that being in your report?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: I remember that line, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: And do you recall stating at paragraph 13 that: "Despite the routine claims of the HVO there are no known or suspected atrocities that have been conducted by the Mujahedin."

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Yes, I wrote that line. I remember it well. And that was my perception at the time. Again, having been in the theatre two months.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Were you aware at the time of other brigades within the Bosnian army, not within the area of the 3rd Corps, which also were referred to as Muslim brigades?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: There was one in the 1st Corps in Sarajevo, was there not? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: I can't, but I would fully accept that there was probably one, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: And one in the 2nd Corps in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: I think I do remember that one, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: And other brigades in the 4th Corps in Konjic and Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Could be. I would accept probably so.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: And one in the 6th Corps.

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Again, I would accept that probably were.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: And they were manoeuvre units or assault units. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: I can't as such, no. I can't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: But the use of the term "Muslim" with brigades was quite common within the Bosnian army.

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Looking at the area of the -- the 3rd Corps. In your report - Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. you may need to refer to it, but perhaps we can do it without wasting time - there were a number of assault brigades, as you called them that you recorded.

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: The 17th Krajina Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: 305 Brigade.

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Yeah, and 7 Janja.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: And 27th Banja Luka Brigade?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Banja Luka, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: And you said that these brigades were combat indicators.

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: That they seldom did defence work but, instead, focussed on assault operations.

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Correct. I think that was most specifically so of 7 and 17.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Were generally offensive -- used in the offensive role, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: So there was more than one brigade that was used in the offensive role that served as a combat indicator for you.

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Yes, 7 and 17 were the two that I followed most carefully, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: And you've also mentioned the forming of an 8th Brigade, the El Mujahed Brigade.

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Moving on to your chart, which is at the back of the report. Once again, perhaps we can take this without --

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: -- it necessarily being in front of you. You have accepted that the information on here might be inaccurate because it might have changed over time.

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: So it wouldn't surprise you, then, if the commander of the Travnik Battalion - you've said that person is Assim Korcic - there's been some dispute over the spelling - was never the commander of that battalion and in fact there were three other persons who were the commanders during the time of 1993/1994.

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: I would fully accept, and it would now not come as a surprise to me, not now nor indeed then, that the "X" of the information was in the box, if you like, or on the chart as at that time as we understood it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: This wasn't a chart that you'd prepared -- and it might be difficult for you to answer questions therefore about it, but I'm seeking to clarify the accuracy, as you can understand, of the report. Is that right that, this is a chart prepared by others?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: I understand the question. Correct, it was a spreadsheet chart prepared by the British Battalion of which we had copies and I would amend as new information came in.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: So we each had copies and free-flowed the information between. Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Moving on to the 2nd Battalion in Zenica. It wouldn't surprise you if the person named there was in fact only an ordinary foot soldier, Mr. Pasanovic, and not the commander indeed of that battalion?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: That would surprise me, only in the fact that that would seem to be a gross inaccuracy from a report from the ground. But I can accept it might be possible, but it would be surprising.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: His name might have come from one particular source, though, that might not have been verified; is that right?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: It would be very unusual to place a name of a commander in a box such as that if it was only on one pure unsubstantiated report. Unusual. I would not say impossible, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: So it would be possible?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: And in respect of Mr. Catic, then, that he was not the commander after June of 1993 of the 3rd Battalion.

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: I could accept that's possible, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: The 7th Brigade, as you recall it, only had three battalions, those that I've mentioned now, and the others that I mentioned on this chart were in fact never confirmed, is that right?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Yeah, that is correct, though I think it important to -- to just highlight that the understanding of a clinical hierarchical structure, as in most regular armies, it was not necessarily the case in the Bosnian army structure or the HVO or -- or anyone, but yes, I accept that the Maglaj Battalion, for example, pictorially displayed on the map, may not have been at Maglaj, and I accept that the Sarajevo Battalion, about which little was known, may not have existed in the way that we -- we depicted it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: And it might be that these two, the 4th and 5th Battalions, were in fact confused with other Muslim brigades, such as those that I mentioned earlier, operating outside of the area of 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: That, it would be possible, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Moving down under the Travnik Battalion, Mehurici. Mehurici is mentioned twice on this chart; there and under the 8th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: There's the name Abu Haris mentioned.

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: He is mentioned under the Mehurici company, I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: But not under the 8th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Yes. The way you understand this chart is that both were based in Mehurici?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Yes. Though, again, to clarify, we were very content that Abu Haris and the Mujahedin, that that core grouping of Mujahedin were based in Mehurici. It was only clarified by your learned friend with the document which she showed me that we had had a report that 8th Muslim Brigade were forming up and that their headquarters was at Mehurici. That was -- it was forming in that period October/November of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that this chart could be inaccurate regarding the Mehurici company and where it fitted in on account of what you said earlier on about the greyness surrounding the subordination of the Mujahedin within the Bosnian army?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: One of the few things that I feel entirely certain about was that the Mehurici headquarters of those Mujahedin -- the core element of Mujahedin, that it -- their headquarters was at Mehurici. I feel certain about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Though I do accept that we were not able to see necessarily the full picture of who was subordinate to whom within the Bosnian army in all matters, no. That I would accept.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you. One final question relates to a document. This is the only document we seek to introduce. And it comes from, Colonel Chambers, your disks which were taken off, I presume, your computer and which were disclosed by the Prosecution to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: I have copies of the document for Your Honours and, of course, for the Prosecution and the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: It's a document dated the 15th of November regarding the Bosnian command reporting requirements. Is this a document that you prepared as part of a briefing session for those collecting information? Can you recall? They were obtained from your disks.

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: I am just trying to remember it. I'm working hard at this now. And as to why it would have been done, I have a very, very vague recollection of it, and I can't remember why it was created. It looks as though we were -- we had some form of G2 conference on the 15th of November with our battalion milinfo officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: And this was one of the presentations or something. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Was that the kind of activity that you engaged in, giving guidelines to those who would be collecting information for your office so that you could prepare your reports as accurately as possible to be passed on to governments?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Yeah. But indeed, this -- looking at it now, just getting a feel for it, it looks like it's the -- if you like, the introductory brief to a new unit and their milinfo team as part of, say, a whole day of instruction of which this was the -- the introduction or overview of the study day, where we are giving them the idea of what it is that we require of them. That's what it appears to me now to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Yes. If you could turn to page 2 of the document, under heading "Assessment and presentation," where you are here referring to the assessments to be put into the reports.

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Yes, I'm reading it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Would you confirm that it's written there: "That that is a matter up to you, no standard format, though area by area works well. Don't worry what it looks like. Doesn't matter if it is not a staff school production."

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: And that further down another point in the presentation: "Try to make a gut feeling assessment at the end daily."

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: And below that: "Try to sum up the week, a seven-sentence sound bite," which is in inverted commas.

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: And the last point: "Don't worry if you are wrong. We often are, and nobody notices."

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Can you confirm that this is a presentation that was given by yourself or those involved in the preparation of milinfosums on 15 November 1993?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: I can't.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please make pauses between questions and answers for the benefit of the interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't. Though I accept that it is quite likely that this presentation was given.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: And would you accept that this was a document retrieved from your computer disks, information kept on your computer?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Almost certainly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel Chambers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Dixon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the most important part was missing, which is for the document to be tendered as an exhibit on the basis that the witness has identified that it was part of the documents that he handed over to the Prosecution, and he has commented on the document today. I'm grateful, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The Trial Chamber would like to thank you for having used only the time allocated to you. Mr. Withopf, as far as the document is concerned, what is the Prosecution's position? This document has been identified -- recognised by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Madam Registrar, could we have an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The exhibit number is DK10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Withopf, is there any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: There is a re-examination, Mr. President. It will be very brief. I have four issues to address; two of them are for clarification purposes only. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Sir, question number one: You already mentioned that your report of the 2nd of November, 1993, was a fusion, to use the word you used, of a report that was put together by Captain Whitley, who was in the area from April to September 1993; it was a fusion of such information and your own information which you could have obtained only after you arrived in September 1993; and you also mentioned in addition, of reports sent to you by the British Battalion. Can you please inform the Trial Chamber as to what point in time the reports of the British Battalion that finally formed part of your report, on what point in time such information was collected.

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Yes. The British Battalion at the time that I was there, who had been there from April through until the October, was the first battalion, the Prince of Wales' Own Regiment, and so they were -- had had six months in which their milinfocell had been able to assess, and at the time that I compiled a report in November, they had just left or were leaving the theatre of Bosnia back to Germany, and so they had six months' worth of collation of that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: For clarification, does it mean that your report was based on information that was collected by the British Battalion between April and September 1993?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Mainly that is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: The second issue, sir: When you were shown the ECMM report dated the 27th of October, 1993, which is Prosecution Exhibit P176, on page 27, line 17 you said that: "This is only a small piece of a big picture." What was the big picture about?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: I've only seen that report today, and I do recall making that statement. I can't remember what it was in relation to. I think it was to do with the taking of a hostage of one -- was it not by the Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: It was the issue about the subordination of the Mujahedin. And you said, "This is a small piece of a big picture." And the question is: What was the big picture about?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Yes. I understand now. The -- the big picture, if you like, is trying to understand, as we spent considerable time and effort trying to understand, where 7 Muslim Brigade fitted into the Bosnian army picture. It was our opinion at that time that 7 Muslim Brigade were receiving, if you like, operational direction from the highest levels of the Bosnian army to conduct operations, predominantly offensive operations, throughout Central Bosnia-Herzegovina. However, again, as part of the bigger picture, is that they lived mainly in the 3rd -- Bosnian 3rd Corps area and received probably logistical support - fuel, weaponry support, transport, and so on - and came under a loose administrative grouping of Bosnian 3rd Corps, though it is accepted, or we certainly came to understand that they were directed in their operational actions from army-group level.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Does it mean that the big picture is actually the one which you included -- or the information which is included in your 2nd of November, 1993 report?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: If you mean by that the diagram as being the big picture of 7 Muslim Brigade, that diagram is, as we understood, the structure of 7 Muslim Brigade at that time being subordinate to Bosnian 3rd Corps for matters, for administration, and all the things I have said; however, fully accepting the fact that they received operational direction from a higher level. So that is the big picture to which I was referring.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Earlier on today you were mentioning, sir, that the ORBAT was part of a spreadsheet, the ORBAT which forms part of your 2nd November 1993 report. Do you recall, and if so can you inform us, as to when this spreadsheet was put together?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: I certainly know that the British Battalion between April and September had this spreadsheet showing all the Bosnian army corps, brigades, battalions as they knew it, and what you are seeing on that chart, as I explained on Friday to the Court, is the -- the extreme right-hand side just 7 Brigade coming underneath of Bosnian 3rd Corps. To the left of that visible chart that you have would be a number of other brigades and units as part of the spreadsheet.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Does this answer imply, sir, that the ORBAT also reflects the situation between April and September 1993?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: It represents a compilation of the situation between April and September 1993, and I will accept and have accepted with your learned Defence counsel that there may have been inherent inaccuracies that were -- or not updated parts of that chart.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And the very last issue, sir, which I wish to address with you: The Defence for Hadzihasanovic has shown you quite a number of documents that had included comments made by representatives of the ABiH. The question is, Lieutenant Colonel, at the time in respect to the reliability of information, did you make a difference between information gathered from independent sources, meaning not the warring factions, and the warring factions?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Yes. The -- we always regarded as -- regarded reports given to us by the warring factions -- any of the warring factions, leaders, or commanders as being -- we used to take the default setting that it was not true unless we were able to prove it to be otherwise true. From reports that we received from other sources, UNPROFOR, non-governmental organisations, and so on, reports that they had seen were taken as true, default setting, unless proved not to be true. However, many of the reports that we received from UNPROFOR and from the non-governmental organisations were from talking to local people. Consequently, we were very sceptical of any information that we received in any report and generally until we had two or three reportings from different sources, we did not accept that to be -- any particular fact to be true.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Withopf. Witness, there are a few questions I would like to put to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before you were sent to Bosnia-Herzegovina, you said that you held a number of positions. It appears that you are an intelligence expert. Is it your previous position that relative to the fact that you were assigned to the headquarters in order to concern yourself with collating information under the authority of a French colonel?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I was -- the entire truth of the matter is I was sent to Bosnia with four days' notice to go because we had run out of people to send. I am -- I was at that time an infantry officer, had just returned from the Toronto -- Canadian Staff College. I was not a specific intelligence expert at that time, and I went there to do the job to the best of my ability as a staff officer. But I did work for Colonel Latapie, a full colonel in the French Army, who was -- himself was not an intelligence expert but had seen service with the French Foreign Legion and was a combat soldier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Today, given your military past, if you had to define "intelligence service," would you say that this should be the matter of specialists or infantry members who are asked to go and gather intelligence and are given four days to be sent on the mission? What could you tell us about this?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Two things, sir: One is that although I was -- I am not an intelligence -- was not then an intelligence expert or specialist, my background in Northern Ireland and -- which was about three and a half years in Northern Ireland, doing various intelligence-related jobs there, predisposed me to be relatively well-trained for this sort of work. Further, my formal training at Sandhurst and on many other courses also trains you to be able to look at the intelligence cycle, as we term it, and to be able to make assessments and create the mechanisms to make assessments. In that regard, although I was not a specialist, I was confident in the manner in which I did my work. However, I have to say that in an ideal world, intelligence specialists or intelligence is best left to intelligence specialists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for that answer. Yesterday you said that the purpose of collating information was only to protect humanitarian convoys and to provide your superiors with information. As far as the protection of humanitarian convoys are concerned, within the framework of your intelligence work, were you aware of any humanitarian convoys that had been attacked, looted, or were parts of any convoys robbed? And if that was the case, by whom?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It was a relatively common or frequent occurrence, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. particularly in the area of Gornji Vakuf, in the southern end of the 3rd BiH Corps's area. However, the main protagonists, people that were shooting at the humanitarian aid convoys, were the HVO in the area of Gornji Vakuf. We had a number of other instances where humanitarian aid convoys became embroiled in a conflict, and one in particular I remember was in the centre of the Vitez pocket between Novi Travnik and Vitez, where a -- an attack was going on, and mortar fire killed two of the truck drivers in -- in Vitez. Further, in my own headquarters at Kiseljak we lost a Belgian corporal who was killed, shot by a sniper, and a Dutch soldier, who was injured in the same truck whilst coming back into the Kiseljak HVO pocket, and we did not know who fired those shots, and it will never be known. So attacks on convoys were relatively frequent, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll go back to the diagram about which many questions and various types of questions were put to you by the Defence. You said that the reports that were compiled were forwarded to the UN, to the ministries of the countries that had troops present in the field, and to other authorities. In your opinion, did these reports have a capital importance in view of the addressees that they were intended for?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Yes. The -- obviously our -- the headquarters that commanded us was Headquarters UNPROFOR in Zagreb. They, of course, needed to know what was happening in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And our military information summary and the pictorial information summary on the Sunday was their prime means of receiving intelligence information on the warring factions in Bosnia and Herzegovina. They were our prime customer, if you like. Other customers were all the other battalions and units within Bosnia-Herzegovina, so that they could read our assessments and try and predict where confrontation would happen. Further, each national government or Ministry of Defence were interested in keeping a watching brief, a watching eye, on what was happening in Bosnia-Herzegovina as it affected their own troops, or indeed may have affected foreign policy decisions by governments and been part of that build-up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In such conditions, any errors [realtime transcript read in error "area"] were excluded or should be excluded given the importance of such reports. Colonel Latapie in the headquarters and his superior, did you inform them of the fact that it was necessary to compile reports which reflected as accurately as possible the reality and did you inform them that any errors should be excluded, even if this was intelligence that was concerned? Mr. Withopf, is there something that's missing?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, it appear that is in line 1 of your question there's something wrong with the transcript. It's written "any areas were excluded," whereas, I understood that you were asking "any errors that were excluded."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. What I wanted to say is that given the importance of your reports, your superiors in headquarters, did they inform you of the risk of making errors and of the fact that it was necessary that these reports reflect as accurately as possible the reality on the ground and this should exclude interpretation of any kind? Were you made aware of this or not?

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Yes, I -- I was. And it is something that in the whole intelligence world people are acutely aware of. And the reason for that is you have a clear choice: You either say nothing and nobody would then know anything; or you have to make a judgement as to what is probable and therefore what is going -- what is useful. And thus, you have to make a judgement call all the time as to how much to include and how much to exclude from a report based on the probability of what you perceive to be happening on the ground, to make a useful assessment. So everybody in the whole community realises that any report is -- is a fusion, a blend, and an assessment, and will not necessarily be straight and absolute fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said that there were 24 liaison officers in the field. Did you have contact with these liaison officers in order to verify the contents of these reports? Did you have discussions concerning the problems with them, or did you quite simply not see them at any time, since these liaison officers were naturally in contact with the local population and with the HVO or BH army units? Did you see them? Were there any working meetings that you had with them concerning your assessment of what was happening, since that was your mission? Your mission was to assess what the reality was.

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Absolutely, sir. Yes, I did meet some of the United Kingdom liaison officers. But to make things completely clear, the three battalion areas that I looked after each had a military information cell. Those cells were receiving information from many sources, and they were the first filter, the first people to collate, assess, and then send to me. So already by the time I am receiving reports from the three battalions, that information has been collated, has been substantiated, where possible, and has been assessed. My job, if you like, was then to take those three reports, or three big elements, and fuse those together to make the picture just that little bit bigger. I did, however, meet some of the liaison officers, and the 24 United Kingdom liaison officers, who were all captains, were specific to the British Battalion. No other battalion had these characters, these officers. So when the British Battalion went in, it had a full battalion of manpower, plus 24 captains whose sole job was to gather information. So the information we received from the British Battalion was inevitably much more than anywhere else. However, those United Kingdom liaison officers reporting to the British Battalion in Vitez would of course have spoken to local commanders, HVO, BiH, and local civilians to inject their reports into the British Battalion in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And my last question: Given the presence of two or 300 Mujahedin, as you have said, now, you said that they were located in Mehurici, did your superiors address this issue and did they think of having a liaison officer within the 7th Brigade? If that wasn't done, in your opinion why wasn't it done, given the importance of the 7th Brigade in general -- in the general framework? And you have referred to this in your report.

utterances.speaker: GUY PHILIP CHAMBERS
utterances.text: Indeed, sir, yes. I would agree, sir. I am not aware of a specific liaison officer or liaison officers who dealt with the 7th Brigade, and I don't know who did liaise with them -- who did liaise with them routinely. I am unsure. I know that a lot of the discussion about the 7 Muslim Brigade and the Mujahedin was had, as indeed some of the documents that have been presented to me today will prove, was had by the then-Lieutenant Colonel Williams talking to Alagic, Enver Hadzihasanovic, and so on. So much was discussed about 7 Muslim Brigade. I am not aware of a liaison officer, and yes, I would agree with you, sir, a liaison officer would have been ideal. I do not know why there was not one provided, or indeed there may well have been. I'm not aware of one though, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. As the Defence took a lot of time, unfortunately the Judges would like to ask you other questions but we can't go beyond the time we have, unfortunately, given the fact that the Trial Chamber has asked the witness a number of questions, is there -- are there any other issues to be raised by either of the parties? Mr. Withopf, is there any issue you would like to raise? The questions were precise and the answers were precise, too. Is there anything you would like to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Nothing from the side of the Prosecution, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Does Defence have any questions for the witness, any brief questions following the answers we have been provided with?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Dixon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Witness, thank you for having spent over two days here, because you spent the weekend in The Hague. You have answered the questions put to you by the Prosecution, by the Defence, and by myself. I would like to thank you for that. And we wish you a good trip home. I will now ask the usher to escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will now adjourn. As we have already said, tomorrow we will be dealing with the documents according to the plan that I mentioned on Friday. I hope that the Prosecution is prepared, as well as the Defence. To the extent that this is possible, we will see if the Prosecution will be in a position tomorrow to have a witness here for Thursday; if not, we'll have to cancel this witness if the discussion of the hearing takes more time than planned. I'd like to stress the fact that both parties should be as concise as possible; they should present the problems very clearly, in order to enable us to move ahead rapidly tomorrow and on Wednesday, because as you know, the Trial Chamber has to render a decision concerning the admissibility -- the admissibility into evidence of the documents contested by the Defence. I think that the Defence is equally well prepared for this debate tomorrow. At this point in time, would either of the parties like to make any comments? Mr. Withopf, is there anything you would like to say, or not to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Could we please go into private session? This is in respect to one witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll go into private session, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in open session now. It is ten past 7.00. I will close the proceedings for today, inviting all parties to come back tomorrow at 9.00 a.m. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 27th day of April, 2004, at 9.00 a.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
